term: "Caching"

## Simple explanation

Caching is the practice of keeping a reusable copy of data or a result so
that a later request can be served without repeating the original work.

## Technical explanation

A caching system defines what is cached, how entries are keyed, where they
are stored, and when they expire or are invalidated. Common strategies
include time-to-live expiration, least-recently-used eviction, and
write-through or cache-aside access patterns.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Inference, embedding generation, retrieval, and data preparation can be
expensive. Caching repeated work may improve latency and reduce compute
cost, but requires careful handling of freshness, personalization,
permissions, and changing model or prompt versions.

## How it works

The application constructs a key from inputs and relevant configuration.
It checks for a matching entry; on a hit, it returns the cached value. On a
miss, it performs the underlying operation and may store the result with
an expiration or version marker.

## Practical example

A retrieval application can cache embeddings for documents using a key
that includes both document content and the embedding-model version. If
either changes, the old cached embedding should not be reused as though it
were current.

## Common misconceptions

- Caching is not a substitute for correctness or data invalidation.
- A poorly designed key can return a result for the wrong user or input.
- A cache can increase system complexity and storage cost even when it
  reduces request latency.
